title: ‘Talk To Me’ Backer Head Gear Opens U.S. Arm With Ambitious Indie Investment Plan
full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart Sphere Media & Paul Barbeau Team Up To Bring TV Drama To Quebec Maxine Peake Boards Short Film ‘The Secret Assistants’ Exploring Power Imbalances In The Movie Business Riley Voelkel & Shiva Negar To Voice Adult Animated Comedy Project ‘Above Average’ View All October 28, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Phil Hunt, Samantha Allwinton Head Gear Films EXCLUSIVE: Head Gear Films is opening in the U.S. and company co-founder and CEO Phil Hunt has told Deadline Head Gear US will sink $120M into U.S. indie film and TV in year one. Head Gear exec Samantha Allwinton will run the new unit as Director of Operations. She will be based in Denver and spend time between there and LA. She was previously COO of Head Gear Films, based in London. Before joining Head Gear she was at Ingenious Media. Head Gear majors in independent film, TV and games finance, including government incentives, presales, gap and bridge funding, as well as executive production and packaging. It has recently helped finance The Apprentice , Talk to Me and How to Have Sex . Related Stories News New AFM Summit To Explore Federal Production Tax Incentive Politics Federal Film & TV Tax Credit Bill Adds Eight New Senate Co-Sponsors The Head Gear US office is opening its doors as a new proposed federal tax credit, part of the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, is moving through Congress. It would apply on top of new and existing state-level incentives. Watch on Deadline Hunt said he wants Head Gear to be in position as the aforementioned industry-boosting measures take effect, which he expects to happen by year-end. “Over 50% of our deal flow is American movies, so we’ve already laid that down. The reason to go to LA is to increase that flow because the federal tax credit’s coming in, which is nice timing. It’s about having more of a foothold in the U.S. and being on their time zone.” He added: “U.S. producers will have half their budget covered and still need the rest. We’ve closed that gap on close to 600 films. We want to be there before the rush.” Head Gear is using existing resources for its U.S. expansion and will provide various types of finance. “When we look at where the company is at right now, and all the other companies that we’re horizontally integrated into, they’re growing. We have got money that we can deploy,” Hunt said. The Head Gear team are regular visitors to the U.S. and Hunt made the point that having a full-fledged base there has been a long-held ambition. “I’ve been meaning to open up in the States for a very long time. I’ve never found the right person until now, who’s got exactly what Head Gear needs and understands Head Gear’s character and ethos, which is quite different from that of most people.” The newly-minted Head Gear US will be at AFM in November and then Sundance in January. “Independent producers need partners who understand their projects and know how to make the numbers work,” Allwinton said. “That’s what we’ve built Head Gear on and it’s what we’re bringing to the U.S. I’m looking forward to sitting across the table from American filmmakers and helping turn their most ambitious ideas into finished films and series.” Production Focus Hunt co-founded Head Gear in 2002 with Compton Ross, who as well as his film interests has been a CEO in the international oil and gas industry for 48 years. With the U.S. office opening, Hunt also spoke about his wider strategy for the business and plans to boost Head Gear’s production-side role. “We’ve been silently kind of working on the production side of Head Gear, and the next phase for us as a business is going back into production and really kind of being the producer’s producer. So, working for the producer in the background; they’ve developed projects, and then we help package them up, do the business affairs, get them off the ground, run finance plans, and then years down the line, we’re still helping collect the money.” Hunt said Head Gear is helping to fund about 30 movies a year and is a hands-on exec producer on a third of those. “Coming from a ‘failed’ producer background, I’m really fascinated with helping producers and guiding them through the marketplace better than ever using our data.” Hasan Piker Sues CNN’s Scott Jennings For $72.5M Over “Manipulated” Video ‘Star Trek’ Vets Reunite For Sci-Fi ‘Life 2.0′; Stephen Fry & Jane Horrocks Comedy Set Russell Brand Forcefully Denies Charges As He Gives Evidence In Rape Trial How ‘Klara And The Sun’ Got Blotted Out At the Box Office With Gloomy Opening Read More About: Comments

title: How “Toxically Optimistic” Zainab Johnson Found a Fan (and Hype Woman) in Michelle Obama
full_text: × Skip to main content By Mikey O'Connell Plus Icon Mikey O'Connell Senior Entertainment Editor View All October 28, 2026 6:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Zainab Johnson Netflix “Washington, DC, make some noise for Zainab Johnson .” The intro itself isn’t an original way to start Johnson’s latest special, Netflix’s Toxically Optimistic , but the individual speaking as she takes the Howard Theatre stage marks a comedy first. That’s Michelle Obama riling up the audience. Johnson, the actress and stand-up who saw her comedy profile surge with 2023’s Hijabs Off , didn’t just get the former former First Lady to introduce her special. The Obamas’ Higher Ground produced the hour, out Oct. 27, a first for their ever-expanding company. So how did Johnson get into business with the Mrs. Obama? By accidentally kind of snubbing her a few years back. Related Stories TV Angry Golf Bros Tried to Ruin Heather McMahan. She Released a Hulu Special Instead Movies Harvey Keitel Threw 'Bad Lieutenant' in the Trash Before Giving One of His Greatest Performances Johnson was in Detroit for a show in late 2024, not far from where Kamala Harris was stumping for her presidential run. Obama was set to attend the rally, so when her team engaged Johnson about meeting her there, Johnson jumped in a car and headed that way. “But I didn’t know how political rallies work,” says Johnson. “I thought you just pull up, park and walk in. No, they shuttle you from a mall that’s ten miles away. I get there and realize I only have enough time to turn around if I’m going to make it to my show. I tell her people that I’m so sorry. And they’re like, ‘Are you sure? Because Michelle is really looking forward to meeting you.’ I know this sounds crazy, but I gotta go be a professional comedian.” Fortunately for Johnson, she’d get another chance a few weeks later —an encounter that’s since proven quite fruitful. Speaking during a recent episode of The Hollywood Reporter podcast I’m Having an Episode (listen to the complete interview on episode on Spotify , Amazon Music , Apple ), Johnson talked about finding a champion in Mrs. Obama, confusing U.K. audiences with a bit about her decision to buy a gun and the billboard she recently spotted that told her all she needed to know about TV’s backslide into defaulting to white actors. So how did you meet Mrs. Obama after this near-miss? In 2024, when Kamala Harris was campaigning, I was in Atlanta when Michelle was there for this bipartisan “Get out the vote” thing. A lot of powerful women in Hollywood were in this room — Kerry Washington, Shonda Rhimes — and I had just had this encounter with these celebrity girls. I was like, “Hey y’all, I’m a fan!” They looked at me like I was dirt. I will not say their names because I’m a huge fan of theirs. I don’t want the world to turn on them. So, I sat down, like, “I don’t know how I got in this room, but let me sit my ass down.” As soon as Michelle walks in the room, everybody flocks to her. She turns, sees me and she says, “Zainab Johnson!” She pulls me up to hug her. She turns me around to Shonda Rhimes, like, “Did you see this girl’s special? It’s fantastic!” She just starts raving about me. In my mind, I’m like, “My God, this is crazy.” Please tell me the women who blew you off were watching as all of this happened. Yes, they saw it. Right after they see Ms. Michelle fawning over me, they come back and apologize. It’s like a high school movie. Like a Mean Girls short starring Zainab Johnson, Michelle Obama and three beautiful, famous girls that will remain nameless. This is the first comedy special produced by the Obamas. I picture you walking into a general meeting, someone handing you a bottled water and Michelle and Barack just hanging out in a conference room. But I’m guessing that’s not how it happened. It’s so far off, not that I haven’t been to Higher Ground for some meetings been offered a wonderful bottle of water. So let’s fast forward to the top of 2026. My team and I decide I’m doing this special. I don’t care if I’m producing it or funding it myself. I’m not gonna wait on anybody to give me permission to put this out. But I had this idea as I was watching Sheng Wang’s special. I’ve always liked how Ali Wong sets the table for him. I thought, “Dang, if somebody were to introduce me, who would I want it to be? What if I got Michelle Obama to do it?” So I called my managers and said, “I’m gonna ask Michelle Obama to introduce my special.” Just voice of God. That’s all I need. I don’t need her to show her face. I don’t need her to produce it. I’m gonna do this thing all by myself. Which is not what happened. Maybe like a week or so later, I’m out to dinner with my friend, and, Michelle’s team, I get a text from them. “Hey, she’s recording the intro right now.” Simultaneously, I get a phone call from my managers. “Yes, she’s recording it. They want to produce the special. How do you feel about that?” I’m having all of the emotions. So they’re like, “Hello?” My friend who’s at dinner with me is asking what’s happening because she can see my face is stunned. And I’m like, “I would absolutely love that.” So then managers start screaming. And when I tell my friend, she says something so interesting to me. She asked how did this happen? “I just asked her to intro me.” She said, “You know what? That’s God, the universe, whatever you want to call it, telling you you can ask for more.” Something I learned about you in this special is that you bought a gun, at your friend’s suggestion, when you moved into a new house. How did the experience of buying a gun compare to how you thought it would be? When they were like, “Get a gun,” I’m thinking we gonna go get a gun with no serial number. I’m thinking we’re getting a back alley gun, right? No. When you go the legal route in California, you have to take classes, you have to get certified, then you have to go to the gun range with a with a certified person. I had to take a test. This used to be in my set, because this this set has come a long way. But I used to talk about how in California, you take a 20-question multiple choice test. I got two of the questions wrong, and they still gave me the gun. That you can get up to five questions wrong and they still give you a gun. That margin of error is crazy to me. And that bar is significantly lower in many other states. When I was touring this through the South, they were like, “Girl, just go to a Walmart! A gas station! Just make sure you have your driver’s license.” Then it was “Girl, you don’t even need that! Just make sure you got the money.” So this went through several incarnations, but you performed an early version at Edinburgh Fringe. This made me wonder how the U.K. audience responds to gun material versus a U.S. audience? The headline of one British paper’s review was “U.S. comic targets gun culture.” It was a bit different in Edinburgh, but I would not have described that show as “she takes on guns.” What’s interesting is that I didn’t just tour it in the U.K., I toured it in Paris. I brought it to Australia, a lot of places where civilians are unfamiliar with day-to-day gun ownership. I remember I would cold open the show with, “I got a gun.” A lot foreign audiences, they would feel confirmed about America with Donald Trump, like, “Yup! We knew it.” Slowly, they’d see some of the material that’s in the special now and they’d be like, “Well, if everybody who has a gun is like you, I guess it’s OK?” With a lot of people, I’m able to get them to see how I’m seeing things. The Edinburgh audience is an older audience. So when I would be like, “I got a gun,” they would be like “ha ha ha” and literally reach for their partner. Then I’d say, “I mean, I don’t have it on me. I don’t think they would have let me through customs.” Then they would understand, OK, this is gonna be a fun time. During a recent interview, you said that the only person that relates to Black women are other Black women. Knowing that, but also knowing that your audience is much broader, I’m curious how some material played. There’s one bit, during which you recount the potential outcomes of a scary encounter walking down a sidewalk. Predicting your possible death, you say, “I’m a Black woman in America. I’ve got to solve my own murder.” It’s a horrifying statement, because it’s very honest, but you play it for laughs. How did that one land on the road? Yeah, I gotta solve my own murder before I go. That’s painfully true, but that’s comedy, right? You bring levity. I’ve toured this hour in different places and when I drop that line, sometimes I would get a standing ovation. Sometimes I would liberate people in the room. Not just Black women. People who have that awareness and understand that truth. And sometimes, I would bring a really laughing crowd down to a sobering reality. It’d be like, “Wait, my God, that’s terrible.” I’m proud that I was able to convey that. It’s such a powerful thing, to convey that in between the absurdity. I’m happy that it landed and I’m happy that it made the final cut. You’re also an actress, and we’ve been talking a lot at work about how TV opportunities have been cratering for people of color. It’s like Hollywood has completely abandoned this push that, for a little while, actually seemed like it was gaining traction. So as you navigate that part of your career, what are the conversations you’re having about opportunities? What does your team say? The talks have been the same, which is, “There’s so little work.” I’m getting the same amount of enthusiasm and willingness to meet with me and pitch an idea. But that last part? The willingness to spend money, to invest, that’s the part. But entertainment is whatever the world is exhibiting at the moment. This might sound crazy, but I haven’t seen this in a very long time. I was driving up La Brea and I saw a billboard for a procedural show. All five of the cast were just cis white people. I I haven’t seen that in years. It’s very back. And I think I know the show you’re referring to. I couldn’t believe it. I almost had to avoid a traffic accident. Am I seeing what I think that I’m seeing? We’re back in the nineties with Friends . We’re back in those conversations. I think we’re in a time that we can call a regression. We are regressing. It’s scary and it’s sad. This is not specific to the show we’re talking that we will not name. But I think it’s all gonna prove to be very boring. THR

title: Peter Medak, Director of ‘The Ruling Class’ and ‘The Changeling,’ Dies at 88
full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All October 28, 2026 5:39am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Peter Medak J. Quinton/WireImage Peter Medak, the Hungarian-born director who guided Peter O’Toole in The Ruling Class , George C. Scott in the classic ghost story The Changeling and Gary Oldman in the crime thriller Romeo Is Bleeding , died Tuesday in Los Angeles, his family announced. He was 88. Medak made his feature directorial debut on the erotic Negatives (1968), featuring Glenda Jackson in one of her first films, and followed that with the black comedy A Day in the Death of Joe Egg (1972), starring Alan Bates and Janet Suzman in an adaptation of Peter Nichols’ play. Related Stories TV Kevin Bleyer, Emmy-Winning 'Daily Show' Writer, Dies at 54 in Car Crash TV Susan Saint James, 'Name of the Game,' 'McMillan & Wife' and 'Kate & Allie' Star, Dies at 80 He also helmed the British gangster drama The Krays (1990), with Gary Kemp and brother Martin Kemp, both members of Spandau Ballet, as real-life British gangsters; Let Him Have It (1991), featuring Christopher Eccleston and Tom Courtenay in another true story, about a controversial hanging; and Zorro: The Gay Blade (1981), starring George Hamilton. For television, Medak worked on multiple episodes of Homicide: Life on the Street , Hart to Hart and Shelley Duvall ‘s Faerie Tale Theatre and on installments of Breaking Bad , The Wire , Space: 1999 , Magnum, P.I. , Law & Order: SVU , St. Elsewhere , Chicago Hope , House and Cold Case . With Medak calling the shots, O’Toole picked up the fifth of his eight career best actor Oscar nominations for his turn as a British nobleman who believes he’s Jesus Christ and then Jack the Ripper in the dark comedy The Ruling Class (1972). Based on a play by Peter Barnes, who also wrote the screenplay, the film played in competition at Cannes. Martin Scorsese, Steven Spielberg, Guillermo del Toro and Alejandro Amenábar are among those who admire his Changeling (1980), about a grieving composer (Scott) caught in a supernatural mystery involving his new home. Spielberg, in fact, screened the film several times for his crew on Poltergeist to help set the tone for that horror classic, Medak noted in a 2018 interview . “He said, ‘This is what it should be.’ It was a great compliment coming from him, and I know he even has his own 35mm copy of The Changeling , and so does Martin Scorsese,” he said. “It’s lovely to have that, to be on their lists of the greatest ghost stories of all time.” Oldman scored high marks for his performance as a corrupt New York homicide detective involved with a vicious hitwoman (Lena Olin) in Romeo Is Bleeding (1993). In his review for Rolling Stone , Peter Travers wrote that Medak “keeps the action stylish, sexy and fiendishly funny. The film rarely makes a lick of sense, but it’s compulsively watchable.” Alas, Medak also is famous for directing the lamentable Ghost in the Noonday Sun (1974), a comedy about bumbling 17th century pirates that starred the combustible Peter Sellers and Spike Milligan. “Oh, it was probably the biggest nightmare of my life,” he said in a 2007 interview for the DGA. Even though the film nearly torpedoed his career, he chose to revisit the experience by helming the 2018 documentary The Ghost of Peter Sellers . Peter Medak (center) with actors Janet Suzman and Alan Bates on the set of 1972’s ‘A Day in the Death of Joe Egg.’ Courtesy Everett Collection Medak was born on Dec. 23, 1937, in Budapest, Hungary. In 1956, he fled to England during his country’s uprising against the communists, and his aunt, an opera singer, helped him quickly land a job with the Associated British Picture Corp. He started out as an editor, cameraman and assistant director and helped out Fred Zinnemann on The Sundowners (1960). A stint as a second A.D. on The V.I.P.s (1963), starring Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton , led to him in 1963 to sign a seven-year contract at Universal Studios to direct for television in Hollywood and London. After many months of false starts, he made his helming debut with a 1965 episode of ITV/Universal’s Court Martial , starring Bradford Dillman and Peter Graves. He had quite the start to his film career. “My first three movies‚ Negatives , Joe Egg and Ruling Class , were just total perfection for me to make as a young director,” he said in a 2020 interview . In 1973, Medak was asked to direct Death Wish , but when he insisted that Henry Fonda be cast as the lead, Paramount turned to Michael Winner, who hired Charles Bronson for the role of vigilante Paul Kersey. On King’s Road in London that year, he ran into Sellers, who invited him to direct Ghost in the Noonday Sun. “Peter was a nightmare,” he recalled. “It was his project, which he developed for two years before me, and I realized about a month before shooting that he’s never read the script. If you can believe it.” The film was shot on location in Cypress, and its pirate ship broke down daily and had to be towed back to the harbor. Meanwhile, the mercurial Sellers fired the producers and faked a heart attack to get time off. (Days later, Medak was stunned to see a newspaper photo of his star dining with Princess Margaret.) The film was so bad, Columbia Pictures never released it; it finally made its way to VHS in the early ’80s. Medak didn’t direct another feature until The Odd Job (1978), starring Monty Python member Graham Chapman. “I was basically punishing myself unconsciously for not making the greatest success of a film with Peter Sellers and Spike Milligan,” he said. “But it wasn’t my fault. Peter’s terrible, insane, destructive behavior on that film [was the reason it failed].” Medak’s résumé also included the features The Men’s Club (1986), La voix humaine (1990), Pontiac Moon (1994) and Species II (1998) and the 1997 telefilm The Hunchback of Notre Dame , starring Mandy Patinkin as Quasimodo. And his love of music of all genres provided him with opportunities to direct early music videos for artists such as Peter Gabriel and Pink Floyd. Survivors include his children, Christopher, Joshua, Karen and Cornelia, and his grandchildren, Sacha, Marlowe, Ryden, Oliver and Anders. He was married to Catherine Marie La Kermance from 1963 until her death by suicide in 1972; to English actress Carolyn Seymour (she’s the wife of O’Toole’s character in The Ruling Class ) from 1973 until their 1984 divorce; and to opera singer Julia Migenes from 1988 until their 2003 divorce. “If it’s in your blood, directing, you never stop,” he said. “And it doesn’t matter that you’re alone in your mind, dreaming or imagining things, you’re always making a movie.” THR

title: Latvian Oscar Submission ‘Ulya’ Sells Wide Ahead of Opening Tallinn: ‘This Film Is a Blockbuster’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: × Oct 28, 2026 5:07am PT Latvian Oscar Submission ‘Ulya’ Sells Wide Ahead of Opening Tallinn: ‘This Film Is a Blockbuster’ (EXCLUSIVE) 'Ulya' has closed sales to a North America and France, while now the second most-watched film in Latvian history, notes director Viesturs Kairiš By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest Latvian Oscar Submission ‘Ulya’ Sells Wide Ahead of Opening Tallinn: ‘This Film Is a Blockbuster’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago ‘Barbara Forever’ Director Brydie O’Connor on Celebrating a Lesbian Icon Who Did It All – and Getting Support From Christine Vachon 1 day ago ‘Good Girls’ Director on Life in Girls’ Correctional Center in Poland: ‘It Damages You Even More’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Ulya,' Courtesy of Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival International distributors continue to fall for “ Ulya .” The Latvian Oscar submission for Best International Feature Film has closed North America (New Mountain Films), France (Destiny), Italy (Invisible Carpet), Slovakia (ASFK), former Yugoslavia (Five Star Distribution), Estonia (Hea Film), Lithuania (GPI), MENA (Teleview), Finland (Cinema Orion), Poland (1989) and Brazil (Belas Arte). Related Stories Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’ The black-and-white film, directed by Viesturs Kairišs , will open the 30th edition of Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival . It premiered at Cannes’ Un Certain Regard section. Produced by Ego Media (LV), Allfilm (EE), Staroń Film (PL) and Tremora (LT), it’s sold by B-Rated International. Inspired by the life of legendary basketball player Ulyana Semjonova, born in 1952, “Ulya” is not a typical biopic. “I don’t think I could ever make a nice, typical biopic. My interest lies in arthouse films. I wasn’t really thinking about sports either. I wanted to tell a Werner Herzog-esque story about a giant girl living in the countryside,” Kairišs told Variety . Semjonova was known for her size; she stood at seven feet tall. But it also made her a bit of a recluse. “I’ve been wondering how to get into her head. I wanted it to be very, very subjective. To stick to her point of view, we used what we called ‘crazy cameras’ and slightly out-of-focus shots. Finding the landscape of her inner soul was a very concrete task.” It was not Kairišs who came up with the idea of making a film about Semjonova. It was the long-held dream of his lead, Kārlis Arnolds Avots . “When I became the artistic director of the Dailes Theatre, I was looking for actors and he was outstanding. During our first meeting, when I asked him to join our ensemble, he said: ‘You know, I would like to play Ulyana Semjonova.’ Then I forgot all about it,” recalled Kairišs. “In theatre, it’s not unusual for men to play women. It goes back to Shakespearean times. A few years later, he played in my film ‘January’. At one point, while I was resting, I heard Kārlis talking to our DP, explaining this idea to him again. That’s when I realized: It’s a film!” Other collaborators still needed convincing, though. “Everyone wanted us to make a standard biopic. I understand it. It could be a good film, but it wouldn’t be my film. We set out to make a film about a girl and we just had to believe in it.” As proved by a photograph of Semjonova with Kārlis Arnolds Avots, added at the end of the film, she actually gave them her blessing. She passed away in January, 2026. “She trusted us. It must have been strange to have us come over and say: ‘And a boy will be playing you.’ But it quickly became clear why it made sense,” said Kairišs. “I actually saw Kārlis yesterday. He’s been filming [the Viking series] ‘Bloodaxe,’ so he has a long beard and he’s really big right now. But he always felt close to her somehow. He knew how it felt to be treated as a ‘giant’.” Or simply as an outsider. To Kairišs’ surprise, “Ulya” has managed to connect with all kinds of viewers, regardless of their size. “Everyone is struggling with something they want to hide, but it’s probably the best part of who they are,” he said. “We had incredible reactions everywhere in Latvia. This film is a blockbuster – we’re already the second most-watched film in history. It was the same at Cannes, Rome and Los Angeles. None of my previous films have received this kind of response. Even my daughter said to me: ‘It’s about me, too.’ We touched upon something that’s very modern and very universal.” Kairišs added: “There’s so much pressure today to look the same and like the same things. We live in times that try to kill all the difference. Everyone struggles with their identity or feels like a ‘freak’. We just have to learn to trust this freak and embrace it as the best thing about us, rather than trying to get rid of it.” Viesturs Kairišs and actor Kārlis Arnolds Avots Courtesy of Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival Secuoya Studios Taps Carla Gómez to Lead Latin American Development as Regional Expansion Accelerates (EXCLUSIVE) HBO’s ‘Harry Potter’ Music Will Be ‘As Far Away as Possible’ From the Movies; Hans Zimmer Says ‘I Can’t Write Like John Williams’ ‘Girls’ Shocker: Lena Dunham Sets Revival at HBO With Allison Williams, Zosia Mamet, Jemima Kirke Returning ‘Industry’ Season 5 Casts Ben Platt, Russell Tovey ‘Lanterns’ Episode 7 Hits 7 Million U.S. Viewers in Three Days as Season Reaches Average of Nearly 19 Million Globally ‘Harry Potter’ HBO Series Casts Its Arthur Weasley, Moaning Myrtle, Colin Creevey Loading comments...

title: Russell Brand Takes the Stand in Rape Trial: “I Know What ‘No’ Means”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All October 28, 2026 4:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Russell Brand outside Southwark Crown Court on Oct. 28. Courtesy of Getty Russell Brand took the stand for the first time in his ongoing rape and sexual assault trial on Wednesday and revealed that no one else has agreed to testify on his behalf. At London’s Southwark Crown Court, the prosecution has completed presenting its case and Brand’s defense team, led by Ian Winter, is now set to detail its arguments for the jury. The prosecution ran the court through all of the charges against the TV host and comedian, also star of St. Trinian’s and Forgetting Sarah Marshall . He is accused of three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one allegation of attempted indecent assault, with six women alleging offenses dating from 1999 to 2009. The final charge was reduced from indecent assault to attempted indecent assault by the judge, Justice Bennathan, on Tuesday afternoon. Related Stories Movies Jafar Panahi Facing Five Years' Imprisonment in Iran After Being Sentenced in Absentia Movies 'Men in Black' Director Barry Sonnenfeld Joins Short Film 'Serenity,' Set in Funeral Home, as Exec Producer (Exclusive) Among the claims is a woman who says Brand raped her in a Bournemouth hotel room in 1999 following one of his comedy gigs. Another says he grabbed her breasts and pushed her into a toilet in a bar in Soho, where he orally raped her in 2004. A separate woman alleges Brand anally raped her at his home in Hampstead in 2009, after consensual vaginal sex. Brand vehemently denies any criminal wrongdoing. According to Sky News coverage , there was a “significant shift” in the courtroom on Wednesday as Brand took the stand as the defense’s first witness. After taking his oath, his barrister began probing Brand on the “sea of change” brought about in his life after marrying U.S. pop superstar Katy Perry in 2010. “It did,” replied the defendant. “Staggering fame.” Brand was asked about the documentary that prompted the police to first investigate him in 2023 . Made by Channel 4’s Dispatches and followed by allegations in The Sunday Times , the program accused Brand of rape and assault . “It was devastating,” he told his barrister, who then asked: “Were you able to persuade a single person with relevant evidence to come to give evidence on your behalf?” Brand replied: “I have not.” When Winter asked if anyone “would touch him with a bargepole,” Brand said, “No.” He added: “My entire life has been consumed by these allegations. I have devoted myself to these matters.” Winter took Brand through various statements from the complainants, some of whom he remembers meeting and others whom he says he has no recollection of. Winter asked Brand, “Is that something that you normally do? Speak during sex?” His client replied, “Yes … I believe I would have been saying: ‘Am I doing this right, do you like this, is this OK?” Brand said when asked for his opinion on consent: “Consent is a fundamental, essential and necessary, and in many ways more important than sex itself.” He discussed the first complainant, saying he remembered meeting her at the Labour Party conference in Bournemouth in 1999. He told the court he found her “loquacious” and “interesting,” and when asked if there was any truth in her claim that Brand raped her that night in a hotel room, the defendant said: “No.” The prosecution, cross-examining Brand, then suggested he “just didn’t care whether she was interested in having sex with you or not.” Brand refuted that and told them he cared “very much.” He added: “I know what ‘no’ means.” The third complainant says Brand groped her breasts in a bar before pulling her to the toilets and forcing her to perform oral sex on him. He does remember meeting her, he told the court. He said a friend introduced him to the woman, telling him “something like, ‘There’s a bird here who really wants to meet you mate.'” Brand told the court that he would have said to this woman upon meeting her: “‘You’re really, really beautiful.'” “Is there any question you just grabbed her breasts?” Winter said to Brand. “Absolutely not,” he replied, saying the act does not turn him on because it’s “disgusting behavior.” He remembers speaking to the complainant for less than a minute before going to the bathroom to “fool around.” Winter said: “As far as you’re aware, is there any question that she did not consent to going into the cubicle with you?” Brand told him: “There’s absolutely no question.” Winter also asked: “Did your penis enter her mouth at all whilst in the cubicle?” His defendant said, “No.” On the allegation that he anally raped another woman at his North London home in 2009, Brand said after a “memorable” sexual encounter he was “excited and enthusiastic” to see her again. The woman said they had consensual vaginal sex in his bedroom, which Brand recalls. When asked if he had then anally raped her, Brand said: “No.” He was asked if she told him to stop, to which he replied: “No.” The trial could last up to six weeks. THR
